# NPC Wojak

2016Image macro / exploitable characterclassic

Published March 10, 2026 · Updated March 23, 2026

Also known as: NPC meme · NPC · Grey Wojak

**NPC Wojak is a grey, expressionless variant of the Wojak meme character, designed to represent people perceived as lacking independent thought or an inner monologue.** The concept originated on 4chan's /v/ board in July 2016, but the distinctive grey-faced visual didn't appear until September 2018, when it exploded into one of the most politically charged memes of the Trump era[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). After Twitter banned over 1,500 fake NPC accounts and major outlets like The New York Times covered the trend, NPC Wojak became a flashpoint in debates about online political discourse, dehumanization, and the media's role in amplifying niche internet culture[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

[wojak](https://meme.com/memes/topics/wojak) [npc memes](https://meme.com/memes/topics/npc-memes) [4chan memes](https://meme.com/memes/topics/4chan-memes) [culture war memes](https://meme.com/memes/topics/culture-war-memes)

## Overview

NPC Wojak takes the familiar Wojak face and strips it of all emotion. The character is drawn in flat grey with a blank stare, a triangular nose, and zero expressiveness, a deliberate contrast to the original Wojak's signature melancholy[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). The name comes from "non-player character," the gaming term for computer-controlled figures who repeat scripted dialogue and follow predetermined paths[3](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-3).

Loading tweet...

The meme works as an insult: calling someone an NPC means they don't think for themselves, just parrot whatever talking points their social circle feeds them. Visually, the grey emptiness of NPC Wojak communicates this message instantly. Unlike other Wojak variants that express specific emotions, NPC Wojak's whole point is the absence of interior life[2](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-2).

## Origin & Background

Platform

4chan (/v/ board for concept, /pol/ board for visual meme)

Creator

Unknown

Date

2016 (concept), 2018 (visual meme)

On July 7, 2016, an anonymous user on 4chan's /v/ (video games) board posted a thread titled "Are You an NPC?" that laid the conceptual groundwork[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5). The poster theorized that some people operate on autopilot, "autonomously follow group thinks and social trends," and compared them to video game NPCs who can only deliver scripted lines[2](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-2). The post described these supposed NPCs as people who recycle the same "buzzwords and hackneyed arguments" and "make a show of discomfort when you break the status quo"[3](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-3).

This concept sat mostly dormant for two years. Then on September 5, 2018, several threads appeared on 4chan's /pol/ board discussing a Psychology Today article about people who don't experience an inner voice or internal monologue[7](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-7). Commenters quickly linked the lack of inner speech to the NPC concept from two years earlier[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). Two days later, on September 7, a grey-colored Wojak variation started showing up in these NPC-themed threads, giving the meme its now-iconic visual identity[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5).

## How It Spread

NPC Wojak broke out of 4chan almost immediately. On September 10, 2018, Twitter user @SpookyStirnman posted a comic showing a normal Wojak being "converted" into an NPC, captioned "All will be converted"[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5). The image spread quickly and set the template for how the meme would be used: a visual metaphor for ideological conformity swallowing individuality[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4).

Within days, the meme triggered a backlash. On September 14, Twitter user @brightabyss accused people who "refer to living humans as being NPCs" of being fascist, drawing over 170 likes[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5). On September 15, more users called NPC a "dog whistle"[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5). Street artist Lushsux posted an NPC Wojak graffiti piece on Instagram on September 17 that pulled in over 16,500 likes[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5).

Kotaku published one of the earliest media analyses on October 5, 2018, with an article titled "How the NPC Meme Tries to Dehumanize 'SJWs'"[2](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-2). The piece argued the meme reduced political opponents to "objects, pawns, strawmen, tools." This drove an initial bump in search traffic[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). But the real explosion came around October 14-16, when The New York Times covered the meme and Twitter simultaneously banned over 1,500 accounts using NPC Wojak profile pictures[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). Google searches for "NPC" spiked, with "4chan" as the second most searched related term[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1).

On October 17, 2018, InfoWars launched a $10,000 contest for the best NPC-themed meme[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5). The contest announcement hit 4chan's /pol/ board and drew over 300 replies in 24 hours[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5).

## How to Use This Meme

NPC Wojak typically appears in a few common formats:

**Basic insult format:** Replace any person or group you want to mock with the grey NPC Wojak face. The implication is that they lack original thought and just repeat scripted talking points.

**Dialogue format:** Show NPC Wojak speaking in canned phrases that parody a particular viewpoint. Common captions mimic generic political slogans, popular opinions, or mainstream talking points presented as if they were pre-programmed responses[2](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-2).

**Code block format:** Present NPC Wojak alongside mock programming code (if/then statements) that "programs" their responses, reinforcing the idea that their beliefs are algorithmic rather than genuine[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4).

**Conversion format:** Show a regular Wojak being turned into an NPC Wojak, implying that social pressure or media consumption transforms individuals into unthinking followers[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5).

**"I Support The Current Thing" format:** Place NPC Wojak wearing multiple pins, badges, or symbols representing trending social causes to suggest performative rather than genuine engagement[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

The meme works best as a reaction image or in multi-panel comics. Its visual simplicity makes it easy to edit and remix.

## Cultural Impact

NPC Wojak hit a rare threshold where a meme from an anonymous imageboard directly influenced mainstream political coverage and platform policy. Twitter's decision to ban 1,500+ accounts was one of the earliest large-scale enforcement actions against a coordinated meme campaign[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). The incident raised questions about where satire ends and election interference begins, since some NPC accounts spread false voting information ahead of the 2018 midterms[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1).

The InfoWars NPC meme contest produced a winning entry by a creator known as "Carpe Donktum," who made a video edit based on the 1988 film \*They Live\*[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4). Then-President Donald Trump later retweeted a different Carpe Donktum video, and the Iowa re-election campaign for Representative Steve King tweeted an NPC meme targeting Democratic members of Congress[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). These incidents marked one of the clearest examples of meme culture feeding directly into electoral politics.

NPC Wojak also sparked academic interest. The meme became a case study in how internet communities use dehumanizing rhetoric to dismiss opposing viewpoints without engaging them[2](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-2). As one analysis put it, the format made it "easier to imagine they steal elections, that the true and only voice of the people sounds like yours" by portraying political opponents as fundamentally artificial[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4).

On Know Your Meme, NPC Wojak outpaced its parent meme in engagement: by the end of 2019, it had 858,000 page views, 597 images, and 749 comments compared to base Wojak's 787,000 views, 332 images, and 47 comments[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

## Full History

The NPC concept had deeper roots than 4chan. By 2010, members of the LessWrong rationalist community in California were already using "NPC" to describe people outside their subculture, framing outsiders as rule-followers who didn't think critically[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). But it was the 2016 4chan post that turned the slur into a meme with a specific visual language and political charge.

The September 2018 revival owed its timing to a specific intellectual catalyst. Users on /pol/ circulated a Psychology Today article about inner speech research, which found that some people never experience an internal monologue while others do so frequently[7](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-7). The study's finding that inner speech occurred in only about 26% of samples, with massive individual variation, became fuel for the idea that a significant portion of the population literally lacked conscious thought[7](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-7). The leap from "doesn't have an inner voice" to "is an NPC" was pseudoscientific but effective as meme material.

Don Caldwell, Know Your Meme's managing editor, told The Verge he was "perplexed" by the meme's rise. NPC Wojak was born in the gaming community "like so many are," he said, but it was so ordinary that he couldn't believe it picked up the traction it did[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). What made it catch fire was the political context: the meme surged during the heated weeks before the 2018 U.S. midterm elections, and it gave the online right a simple visual shorthand for dismissing progressive arguments[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

The coordinated Twitter campaign was a turning point. Users from Reddit's r/The\_Donald created hundreds of accounts with NPC Wojak profile pictures, posing as exaggerated liberal activists with hashtags like #resist[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). Some accounts crossed from satire into election interference by posting false information about voting dates, telling liberals to vote on November 7 when Election Day was November 6[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). Twitter's subsequent mass ban of 1,500+ accounts only amplified interest through the Streisand effect[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4).

Whitney Phillips, a Syracuse University professor who studies media amplification, identified the exact problem at work. Her research report "The Oxygen of Amplification" examined how press coverage of niche memes inadvertently supercharges them[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). The NPC Wojak saga was a textbook case: relatively few outlets had touched it before The New York Times piece, but that article kicked off a domino effect. Paul Joseph Watson, InfoWars, and other right-wing media figures immediately amplified the meme to their audiences through YouTube videos and tweets[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). A search for "NPC meme" on YouTube at the time returned a flood of videos, most uploaded within the previous week[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1).

Ironically, as Caldwell noted, NPC Wojak was also used as an anti-Trump meme in its early days, dunking on conservatives for their own perceived groupthink[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1). Both left-wing and right-wing versions existed, though the right-wing usage dominated media coverage[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4). One popular variant showed NPC Wojak arguing with itself, and meta versions mocking the meme's own users appeared almost as fast as the originals[4](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-4).

The meme's afterlife extended well beyond 2018. In 2022, a variant called "I Support The Current Thing" went viral, showing NPC Wojak wearing pins and symbols for a rotating cast of causes. According to Slate, the meme mocked liberals for "perceived conformism, frivolousness, and distractibility" in how they shifted from issue to issue[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). Elon Musk tweeted a version of this variant in March 2022, bringing it to an audience of tens of millions[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6). That same year, NPC Wojak found new life on TikTok through "NPC streamers" who acted out robotic, scripted behavior on livestreams, flipping the concept from insult to performance art[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

▼Read Full History

⚠

Sensitivity Note

The NPC meme became heavily politicized in 2018, primarily used by right-wing communities to mock liberals and progressives as unthinking conformists. Twitter banned numerous NPC-themed accounts for coordinated inauthentic behavior. While the concept of 'NPC behavior' (blindly following trends) applies to any group, in practice the meme has been predominantly used as a partisan weapon. Some critics argue it dehumanizes political opponents by literally comparing them to non-human game characters.

## Fun Facts

The September 2018 NPC threads on /pol/ were triggered by a real Psychology Today article about inner speech research, which found some people never experience an internal monologue[7](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-7).

NPC Wojak was used by both the political left and right in its early days, though media coverage focused almost exclusively on right-wing usage[1](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-1).

Street artist Lushsux painted one of the first real-world NPC Wojak pieces on September 17, 2018, just ten days after the visual meme first appeared online[5](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-5).

The term "NPC" as an insult for real people predates the meme by several years, with California's LessWrong community using it as early as 2010[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).

Despite its online origins, NPC Wojak became one of the few memes directly referenced in a sitting U.S. congressman's re-election campaign material[6](https://meme.com/memes/npc-wojak#ref-6).
